::: {.why}
American options are the ones actually listed on single stocks, and the reason a simulation cannot price them directly is worth understanding rather than working around.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Price an American put on a binomial tree and say why the same expectation cannot be evaluated by forward simulation.
- Report the early exercise premium and identify the region where exercise is optimal.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Implement American exercise on your tree by taking the maximum of continuation and intrinsic value at each node, then price an American and a European put on the same parameters and report the premium. Plot the exercise boundary in spot and time.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Say why simulation struggles: the optimal exercise decision at a node depends on the continuation value, which is a conditional expectation of the future, and a forward simulation does not have it. Then read what the standard fix is, which regresses continuation value on state variables across paths, and note that it is a regression on simulated data with all the overfitting risks you already know about.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Check your tree against QuantLib's American pricer to make sure the exercise logic is right.
:::
:::
